name: Lady Sudeley

origin.raised_by: Mr Jacob, a cottager at Petworth

history: Raised around 1849 by a Petworth cottager named Jacob and later introduced by George Bunyard and Co. of Maidstone in 1885, a year after it won an RHS Award of Merit. A showy Victorian garden apple, it is a parent of Benenden Early and Laxton's Beauty of Bedford.

look.description: Handsome, distinctly ribbed fruit, golden yellow boldly striped and flushed with orange-red to scarlet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy yellowish flesh with a lively, slightly sharp flavour of good quality. Best eaten straight from the tree; it softens within about a week.

tree.notes: Average vigour with attractive blossom. The wood is brittle and branches can snap under a heavy crop, so thin fruit and support laden limbs.

pollination.notes: Fairly late-flowering for an early apple (group 4) with frost-resistant blossom; partly self-fertile but crops better with a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central England and similar mild climates; its later, frost-resistant blossom helps in gardens with spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would hasten softening and dull the striped colour; no records from hot regions.

health.other: Reported to have good general disease resistance. Main weakness is brittle wood that breaks under heavy crops.

grow_notes: A decorative early apple for gardens, good in sites where late frosts catch earlier blossom. Thin the fruit in heavy years to protect the brittle branches, and pick over a few weeks from late August.

name: Laxton's Epicure
history: Crossed by the Laxton Brothers of Bedford in 1909 and released in 1929; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1931 and later the Award of Garden Merit. It brings some of Cox's flavour to an apple that ripens several weeks earlier.

look.description: Smallish truncated-conical apple, greenish-yellow streaked and mottled with brownish to bright red.

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy and aromatic, with a fine-grained, moderately crisp texture and something of the Cox richness in it. Flavour is best when the apples are left to ripen fully on the tree, and it fades within a couple of weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep; does not keep long

tree.notes: A rather small, very precocious tree with large leaves that will set fruit even on unpruned one-year shoots. Thin heavy crops to keep fruit size.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3); plant with another group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens such as most of Britain; ripening in late summer, it is picked before autumn weather sets in.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, high-rainfall districts raise the risk of canker; hot summers would give soft fruit with little colour.

health.other: Disease resistance slightly above average overall, but canker can be a problem in wet districts.

grow_notes: A good Cox-flavoured early apple for small gardens because the tree stays compact and crops young. Grow on well-drained soil, thin the fruit, and leave apples on the tree until fully ripe for the best flavour.

name: Maidstone Favourite
history: Raised by the Maidstone nursery of George Bunyard and Co. and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1913. A Kent early apple from the same firm that introduced Lady Sudeley, now rare outside collections.

look.description: Smallish to medium, flattish, very even fruit, pale green-yellow prettily striped with carmine red.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, juicy and sweet, with a pleasant and slightly distinctive aromatic flavour. An apple for eating within days of picking.

tree.notes: Little growing data recorded. Prune as a normal spur-bearing dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early-to-mid season, similar to Beauty of Bath.

climate.best_climates: Kent and similar mild south-east English conditions where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or very cold regions; soft early fruit generally fares badly in hot summers.

grow_notes: A Kent heritage apple for collectors and local-variety orchards. Grow in sun on well-drained loam with an early or mid-season diploid pollinator and pick in mid August.

name: Melba

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: McIntosh seedling; the pollen parent is often given as Liveland Raspberry but is not firmly documented
origin.raised_by: W. T. Macoun, Central Experimental Farm

history: Raised in 1898 by W. T. Macoun at Canada's Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa and released in 1909; it is generally said to be named after the opera singer Nellie Melba. It won the American Pomological Society's Wilder Medal in 1927 and became a leading summer apple in Canada and Scandinavia.

look.description: Pale yellow apple washed and striped with pinkish to crimson red, with a whitish bloom and somewhat ribbed shape.

taste.summary: Snow-white, crisp and juicy flesh that softens fairly quickly, with a sweet, lightly tart, wine-like flavour and the perfumed skin aroma typical of the McIntosh family. Also makes good sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep; eat soon after picking or use for sauce

tree.notes: Very productive and bears young, but strongly inclined to alternate cropping; thin hard in heavy years. Fruit bruises easily.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not reliably published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early-to-mid season, similar to Beauty of Bath.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental and northern climates such as eastern Canada, the northern US and Scandinavia, where it is very winter-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Hot humid summers bring soft fruit, poor colour and heavy scab pressure; mild, wet maritime climates also favour scab.

health.other: Susceptible to scab like other McIntosh offspring; strongly biennial; fruit bruises easily.

grow_notes: One of the hardiest good-quality summer apples, worth growing in cold districts. Thin fruit every year to curb biennial bearing, and spray or choose an open, airy site where scab is common.

name: Miller's Seedling
history: Raised in 1848 by James Miller at Newbury in Berkshire and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1906. Popular with Victorian and Edwardian gardeners as a sweet, juicy early apple; a redder sport, Red Miller, also exists.

look.description: Pale greenish-yellow, flattish apple with a light pink-red flush and fine red stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: White, very juicy flesh, crisp but light when first picked and soon softening, with a sweet, refreshingly tart and fragrant flavour. It bruises at the slightest knock and goes waxy within about a week, so eat it straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: Crops very heavily in its 'on' years and then rests, so thin fruitlets hard to even out cropping.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in early flowering group 2 (one guide gives 3); partly self-fertile but sets better with a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild temperate climates like southern and central England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the soft, easily bruised fruit deteriorate even faster; no records from hot regions.

health.other: Average disease resistance. Main faults are a strong biennial habit and fruit that bruises very easily.

grow_notes: A rewarding sweet early apple for gardens if thinned every year to avoid feast-and-famine cropping. Handle the fruit gently and eat or juice it within a week of picking.
